Time Signatures: Two Ways to Sort Them

The classical grid of simple and compound, duple, triple and quadruple meters, and Music Learning Theory’s usual and unusual meters (duple, triple, combined; paired and unpaired), with a table that translates between them.

There are two common ways to sort meters. Classical theory reads the time signature and sorts by two questions: how many beats in a bar and how is each beat divided. Music Learning Theory (MLT) sorts by what you hear and move to: how the big beats are divided, and whether the big beats are all the same length. The two systems often give different names to the same music.

Click any heading to fold its section.

The classical grid: simple/compound × duple/triple/quadruple

Two questions, two words (Hutchinson, “Meter”):

  1. How is the beat divided? Into two parts: simple. Into three parts: compound.
  2. How many beats in a bar? Two: duple. Three: triple. Four: quadruple.
Duple (2 beats) Triple (3 beats) Quadruple (4 beats)
Simple (beat ÷ 2) 2/4, 2/2, 2/8 3/4, 3/8, 3/2 4/4, 4/2
Compound (beat ÷ 3) 6/8, 6/4, 6/16 9/8, 9/4 12/8, 12/4

The quick rule: if the top number is 6, 9 or 12, the meter is compound, and the beat is a dotted note. Divide the top number by 3 to get the number of beats: 6/8 has two dotted-quarter beats, so it is compound duple. Otherwise the top number is the number of beats: 3/4 is simple triple.

Meters that don’t fit the grid. Signatures such as 5/8 and 7/8 have beats of unequal length (5/8 is usually felt as 2+3 or 3+2 eighths; 7/8 as 2+2+3 or another order). Textbooks call these asymmetrical, irregular or complex meters, and the names vary from book to book (these names are from general use and not yet checked against a source).

The classical question: What does the time signature say? You can answer it by looking, without hearing the music.

The MLT way: usual and unusual meter

Gordon builds meter from two layers you feel in your body: macrobeats (big beats; tap them with your heels) and microbeats (the smaller beats that divide them; tap them with your hands) (Gordon 175).

Usual meter: big beats all the same length

When the macrobeats are equal and come in pairs, the meter is usual. Then the question is how is each macrobeat divided? (Gordon 175–176):

  • Usual duple: each macrobeat divides into 2 microbeats. Chant: du de du de.
  • Usual triple: each macrobeat divides into 3 microbeats. Chant: du da di du da di.
  • Usual combined: some macrobeats divide into 2 and some into 3, while the macrobeats stay the same length.

(Rhythm syllables: Gordon 105.)

Unusual meter: big beats of different lengths

When the macrobeats are not all the same length, the meter is unusual. Now the question is how are the macrobeats grouped? (Gordon 179–180):

  • Unusual paired: two macrobeats in a group, one longer than the other. Five microbeats as 2+3 or 3+2, often written 5/8.
  • Unusual unpaired: three macrobeats in a group, of unequal lengths, such as 2+2+3, often written 7/8. Two of them form a pair and one is left over; the listener decides which.
  • Intact: in unusual paired intact and unusual unpaired intact meters, the macrobeats are felt without being divided into microbeats.

Gordon sums up the difference: “In usual meter, microbeats establish meter, and macrobeats establish tempo. In unusual meter, macrobeats establish meter, and microbeats establish tempo” (Gordon 180).

The meter is heard, not read

Gordon says “there is no direct relation between notation, particularly measure signatures and meter.” He calls the textbook label of 6/8 as “duple compound meter” “inaccurate”: in 6/8 you hear two macrobeats, each divided into three, which is usual triple (Gordon 176). Three more things that, for Gordon, do not change the meter (Gordon 176–177):

  • Tempo: fast or slow macrobeats are still the same meter.
  • Accents: a waltz is usual triple whichever beats a dancer or band accents.
  • Smaller divisions: sixteenth-note triplets in 2/4 don’t make it triple; sixteenths in 6/8 don’t make it duple.

The MLT question: Move to it. Are the big beats equal? Then how many small beats fit in each? You answer it by listening and moving, before you have seen any notation.

The two systems side by side

The same signatures, sorted both ways. The MLT column is what you would usually hear; for Gordon the music, not the signature, decides.

Signature Classical MLT (usually) Why they differ
2/4 simple duple usual duple they agree
4/4 simple quadruple usual duple MLT doesn’t count beats per bar; the macrobeats divide in 2
3/4 (a waltz) simple triple usual triple classical counts 3 beats in the bar; MLT hears one macrobeat per bar divided in 3, paired with the next bar
6/8 compound duple usual triple classical counts 2 beats; MLT names the division of each beat (3)
9/8 compound triple usual triple classical counts 3 beats; MLT hears each divided in 3
12/8 compound quadruple usual triple same reason
6/8 with some beats split in 2 compound duple with duplets usual combined MLT has a name for the mix
5/8 (2+3) irregular / asymmetrical unusual paired MLT asks how many big beats are grouped (2)
7/8 (2+2+3) irregular / asymmetrical unusual unpaired three big beats, one left unpaired

The key difference:

  • In classical names, duple / triple / quadruple counts beats in a bar, and simple / compound names how each beat divides.
  • In MLT names, duple / triple names how each macrobeat divides (that is, what classical theory calls simple and compound), and paired / unpaired counts macrobeats in a group, which only matters when they are unequal.

So the classical word triple and the MLT word triple answer different questions. “Simple triple” (3/4) and “compound duple” (6/8) are different meters in classical theory, but both are usual triple in MLT.

Check yourself

For each, give the classical name and the MLT name. Answers are below.

  1. “Row, Row, Row Your Boat” written in 6/8.
  2. A march in 2/2.
  3. A minuet in 3/4.
  4. A tune in 7/8 grouped 3+2+2.
  5. A jig in 12/8.
TipAnswers
  1. Compound duple; usual triple.
  2. Simple duple; usual duple.
  3. Simple triple; usual triple (one macrobeat per bar, divided in 3).
  4. Irregular (asymmetrical); unusual unpaired.
  5. Compound quadruple; usual triple.

Practise hearing the MLT meters with the Rhythm Patterns and Audiation pages. Related: Modes: Three Meanings of One Word.
